explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. David says, “…save me by Your righteousness.” (Psalm 31:1) The righteousness he's counting on is the LORD's, not his own. He doesn't walk in waving a list of his good deeds.

Right, and look whose righteousness he names. “…save me by Your righteousness.” (Psalm 31:1) That's the LORD's, not David's. A king could point at himself when he needs rescue, and David points at God instead. I think that's a habit worth stealing.

Fortress is the word. David says, “For You are my rock and my fortress…” (Psalm 31:3) A rock and a fortress, two solid things stacked together. When David wants to say safe, he doesn't reach for anything soft.

David never calls the LORD a river in this verse. He says, “For You are my rock and my fortress…” (Psalm 31:3) A river keeps moving, and David picked words that stay put. I think that's exactly why he chose a rock.

A garden sounds lovely, friend, but it's not in this verse. David says, “For You are my rock and my fortress…” (Psalm 31:3) Nobody runs to the flower beds when trouble is chasing them. They run for walls, and walls are what David asks for.

For the sake of His name. David says, “…lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name.” (Psalm 31:3) He asks the LORD to be his guide, and he ties it to God's name. Hand the map to the One who knows the road, baker.
David's family doesn't come up in this verse. He says, “…lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name.” (Psalm 31:3) The name he points to is the LORD's. That one name carries the whole request.

David is king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), so I get why kingdom came to mind. But he says, “…lead me and guide me for the sake of Your name.” (Psalm 31:3) The name is the LORD's, not a crown or a throne. Even a king can be the one who needs guiding.

The LORD. David says, “You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge.” (Psalm 31:4) Somebody set a trap, and David names the One who gets him out of it. That's the third time refuge shows up in four verses, so David is really leaning on that word.

David had mighty men, but they aren't in this verse. He says, “You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge.” (Psalm 31:4) The One he credits is the LORD. I think David knew exactly where to look when the net came out.

Jonathan, King Saul's son, really was a friend to David (1 Samuel 18:1). But he isn't in this verse. David says, “You free me from the net laid out for me, for You are my refuge.” (Psalm 31:4) He gives the credit to the LORD.

Redeemed him. David says, “Into Your hands I commit my spirit; You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth.” (Psalm 31:5) He hands over his spirit and names what the LORD has done in the same breath. Jesus prays that first line from the cross (Luke 23:46).

Money never comes up in this verse, friend. David says, “…You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth.” (Psalm 31:5) That's what he says the LORD has done. I'd take that over a full cookie jar any day.
A son isn't mentioned here. David says, “…You have redeemed me, O LORD, God of truth.” (Psalm 31:5) Redeemed is the word he uses. He says it right as he puts his spirit into the LORD's hands.

True. David says, “I hate those who cling to worthless idols, but in the LORD I trust.” (Psalm 31:6) Watch that little word “but.” On one side are people holding tight to worthless idols. On the other side, David puts his trust in the LORD.

It sounds strong, but it's right there in the text. David says, “I hate those who cling to worthless idols, but in the LORD I trust.” (Psalm 31:6) So the answer is true. And notice the verse ends with where his trust goes.

Affliction. David says, “…You have seen my affliction; You have known the anguish of my soul.” (Psalm 31:7) The LORD saw the hard part, and that's what David is glad about. Being seen in the hard part is no small thing, baker.

No victories in this verse. David says, “…You have seen my affliction; You have known the anguish of my soul.” (Psalm 31:7) If I were picking, I'd have bragged about my best batch. David points at the hard part instead.

Riches don't show up here. David says, “…You have seen my affliction; You have known the anguish of my soul.” (Psalm 31:7) What he rejoices over is that the LORD saw it and knew the anguish. I think that's worth more than money to anybody hurting.

His eyes fail. David says, “…my eyes fail from sorrow, my soul and body as well.” (Psalm 31:9) The sorrow reaches his eyes, then his soul and body too. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the psalm, and David doesn't hide it.
Battle isn't in this verse. David says, “…my eyes fail from sorrow, my soul and body as well.” (Psalm 31:9) The sorrow hits his eyes, his soul and his body. It's a heavy verse, friend.
He isn't turning from God. He's calling out, “Be merciful to me, O LORD, for I am in distress…” (Psalm 31:9) The sorrow hits his eyes, his soul and his body. And all of it goes straight to the LORD.
Bones. David says, “…my iniquity has drained my strength, and my bones are wasting away.” (Psalm 31:10) He names his own iniquity out loud and doesn't dress it up. I think this verse hurts.

David was a shepherd once (1 Samuel 16:11), so flocks are a fair guess. But this verse is about his own body. He says, “…my iniquity has drained my strength, and my bones are wasting away.” (Psalm 31:10) The wasting is in his bones, not in a pasture.

Vineyards aren't in this verse. David says, “…my iniquity has drained my strength, and my bones are wasting away.” (Psalm 31:10) The wasting is happening to him, not to a field. I think this one is a heavy verse.
Not quite, baker. David says, “…they flee when they see me on the street.” (Psalm 31:11) His friends run the other way. I think that's a lonely thing to say out loud.
Right. David says, “…they flee when they see me on the street.” (Psalm 31:11) Instead of hurrying over, his friends head for the exit. I think this one stings.
A broken vessel. David says, “I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind. I am like a broken vessel.” (Psalm 31:12) Two hard pictures, back to back. I think he's saying he feels pretty useless.

A withered tree is a good picture, but it isn't David's. He says, “I am like a broken vessel.” (Psalm 31:12) A vessel is something you carry or pour from, and his has broken. I think he feels cracked all the way through.
A dry well isn't in this verse. David says, “I am like a broken vessel.” (Psalm 31:12) That comes right after he says he's forgotten like a dead man. I think this is a hard verse to read.

True. David says, “They conspire against me and plot to take my life.” (Psalm 31:13) It's the same verse with the slander and the terror on every side. So this is more than gossip. I think David's life is on the line.
It's right there in the text, friend. David says, “They conspire against me and plot to take my life.” (Psalm 31:13) So the answer is true. This verse is a heavy one.

explanations.answer: That he trusts in the LORD
explanations.explanation: He trusts in the LORD. David says, “But I trust in You, O LORD…” (Psalm 31:14) Slander, terror, plots, and then comes that little word “But.” That “But” is doing some heavy lifting, baker.

explanations.answer: That he will fight them alone
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say he'll fight alone. He says, “But I trust in You, O LORD…” (Psalm 31:14) After all that trouble, his next move is trust. No lone hero speech.

explanations.answer: That he will hide in the hills
explanations.explanation: No hiding in the hills here. David says, “But I trust in You, O LORD…” (Psalm 31:14) He turns from the plots straight to the LORD. That “But” is the whole turn.
His times. David says, “My times are in Your hands…” (Psalm 31:15) Back in verse 5 it was his spirit, and here it's his times. Hands again, baker. His spirit and his times both rest with the LORD.
David is king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), so crown is a fair guess. But he says, “My times are in Your hands…” (Psalm 31:15) That's his times, not his crown. The king hands over his days, not his hat.

No sword in this verse. David says, “My times are in Your hands…” (Psalm 31:15) Honestly, I'd trust the LORD's hands over my own with a sword. With my mustache holding it, nobody in the bakery would be safe.
It's the other way around. David says, “Make Your face shine on Your servant…” (Psalm 31:16) He asks for the LORD's face to shine on him, not hide from him. Hiding isn't on his list.
Right. David says, “Make Your face shine on Your servant…” (Psalm 31:16) Shine, not hide. David is asking for the light.

To be silenced. David says, “May lying lips be silenced…” (Psalm 31:18) These are lips full of pride and contempt, speaking with arrogance against the righteous. He basically asks for that group chat to go mute.

Forgiveness isn't what David asks for in this verse. He says, “May lying lips be silenced…” (Psalm 31:18) The lips he means speak with arrogance against the righteous. His request is that they go quiet.
No reward in this verse, friend. David says, “May lying lips be silenced…” (Psalm 31:18) He's talking about lips that speak with arrogance against the righteous. What he asks for them is silence.

Fear. David says, “How great is Your goodness which You have laid up for those who fear You…” (Psalm 31:19) Goodness laid up, like something saved and set aside. That's a storeroom worth knowing about, baker.

Plenty of us question things, friend, but that's not David's word. He says, “How great is Your goodness which You have laid up for those who fear You…” (Psalm 31:19) The word is fear. And the goodness is laid up for them.

Avoid isn't in this verse. David says, “How great is Your goodness which You have laid up for those who fear You…” (Psalm 31:19) The goodness is for those who fear Him. David is cheering about how great it is.

explanations.answer: In the secret place of His presence
explanations.explanation: In the secret place of His presence. David says, “You hide them in the secret place of Your presence from the schemes of men.” (Psalm 31:20) The hiding spot is God's own presence. Best hiding spot I've ever heard of, baker.

explanations.answer: In the deep caves of the hills
explanations.explanation: Caves are a classic hiding spot, and David hid in one once (1 Samuel 22:1). But this verse says something else. David says, “You hide them in the secret place of Your presence…” (Psalm 31:20) The hiding spot is God's presence.

explanations.answer: In the inner courts of the king
explanations.explanation: The inner courts of a king sound safe, friend. But David says, “You hide them in the secret place of Your presence…” (Psalm 31:20) The spot is God's presence, not a palace. I bet that beats any palace in town.

Not a city at peace, baker. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, for He has shown me His loving devotion in a city under siege.” (Psalm 31:21) It's a city under siege. David found loving devotion in the middle of that.

Right. David says, “Blessed be the LORD, for He has shown me His loving devotion in a city under siege.” (Psalm 31:21) A city under siege, not a quiet one. He blesses the LORD for loving devotion right in the middle of it.

True. David says, “In my alarm I said, ‘I am cut off from Your sight!’” and then, “…But You heard my plea for mercy when I called to You for help.” (Psalm 31:22) He said it in alarm, and the LORD heard him anyway. Alarm can do a lot of talking, friend.

Good news, it's true. David says, “…But You heard my plea for mercy when I called to You for help.” (Psalm 31:22) He had said he was cut off from God's sight. Even so, the LORD heard his plea for mercy.
The faithful. David says, “The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant.” (Psalm 31:23) Two groups, two different ends. He says it to all the LORD's saints.
Wealthy isn't David's word. He says, “The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant.” (Psalm 31:23) The ones preserved are the faithful. A fat wallet isn't mentioned.

Clever is tempting, baker. But David says, “The LORD preserves the faithful, but fully repays the arrogant.” (Psalm 31:23) Being clever once got me a cookie stamped upside down. The faithful are the ones he names.

Strong and courageous. The last line says, “Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD.” (Psalm 31:24) After all those heavy verses, David ends by lifting people up. That's a good place to land, baker.

Quiet and patient aren't the words David picks. He ends with, “Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD.” (Psalm 31:24) It's a call to strength and courage. And it's for everyone who hopes in the LORD.

Wise and humble are good words, but they aren't in this last line. David says, “Be strong and courageous, all you who hope in the LORD.” (Psalm 31:24) He wants those who hope in the LORD to be strong and courageous. That's how the psalm ends.
